title: Effects of acute ketone body supplementation on endurance performance in endurance-trained amateur athletes – A three-arm, double-blind, cross-over study
summary:
Ketone bodies, including acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate, are water-soluble organic compounds derived from lipid metabolism and are produced almost exclusively in the liver. Their production is particularly elevated under physiological conditions characterized by limited carbohydrate availability, such as starvation, prolonged fasting, or adherence to ketogenic diets (Robinson, 1980). Various forms of exogenous ketogenic supplements are available, including medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs), (R)-3-hydroxybutyl (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate, R,S-1,3-butanediol acetoacetate, 1,3-butanediol, and ketone salts. These compounds can be administered either individually or in combination with medium-chain triglycerides (Evans et al., 2022).

The proposed mechanism underlying the potential ergogenic effects of exogenous ketone supplementation involves a reduced reliance on carbohydrate oxidation during exercise or competition, commonly referred to as glycogen sparing. Since performance in many team and endurance sports is highly dependent on carbohydrate availability, athletes participating in activities in which performance is limited by hepatic and/or skeletal muscle glycogen stores may benefit from nutritional strategies aimed at preserving endogenous glycogen reserves (Evans et al., 2022).

However, the current scientific evidence regarding the effects of exogenous ketone supplementation remains inconclusive. Different supplementation strategies have yielded inconsistent findings across studies. While Cox et al. (2016) and O'Malley et al. (2017) reported alterations in substrate metabolism following ketone supplementation, these findings have not been consistently replicated in subsequent investigations (Leckey et al., 2017; Poffe et al., 2019; Evans et al., 2019).

Given the potential of targeted exogenous ketone supplementation to enhance exercise performance, alongside the heterogeneous and sometimes contradictory findings reported in the existing literature, the present experimental study aims to investigate the effects of acute exogenous ketone supplementation on exercise performance in recreationally trained athletes undergoing standardized exercise performance testing.

In summary, the proposed benefits of exogenous ketone supplementation include potential improvements in endurance performance and post-exercise recovery, as well as the preservation of endogenous carbohydrate stores. However, the extent to which these effects occur and whether they differ between specific ketone formulations remain unclear. Therefore, the primary objective of the present study is to determine whether different forms of exogenous ketone supplementation exert differential effects on acute exercise performance in recreationally trained athletes.
